Special sessions will concentrate on engine tribology, wear of tools and tooling materials, friction and wear under vibratory contact, marine applications, role of third bodies during wear, and surface texturing for wear reduction.

DSL.TITLE: Engaged Scholar & Artist Award: Multidisciplinary study of vegetable oil-based nanol-ubricants with enhanced properties
DSL.COMMENT: Crude oil-based lubricants are both harmful to the environment and increasingly scarce. Vegetable oil-based lubricants make a fitting substitute because they have natural esters (biodegradable material) to attract them to metals. Nanoparticles, which are small particles undetectable to the eye, elevate the effectiveness of these lubricants by allowing surfaces to slide across each other easily, having the nanoparticles act as a protective film, filling cracks in crevices, and pushing small fragments off surfaces. To make vegetable oil-based lubricants practical beyond the lab, this project aims to prevent nanoparticles from settling to the bottom of the solution over time, and address health risks of manufacturing the lubricant using nanoparticles. Additives will be introduced to the lubricant solution and tested against old formulas so sedimentation can be observed over time. The performance of the new developed nanolubricant (nanoparticle-based lubricant) will be experimentally evaluated using a previous developed methodology.

CONGRANT.TITLE: ERI: Fundamental understanding of vegetable oil-based nanolubricants for industrial applications
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Project Summary

Overview:
The objective of this research project is to acquire fundamental understanding of the effects of different types of nanoparticles, surfactants, and concentrations on the rheological behavior, thermophysical properties, and tribological performance of vegetable oil-based nanolubricants. According to new studies, about 23% of the world´s energy consumption is spent to overcome friction between moving components and to replace or repair worn tooling and materials. In the context of energy efficiency, the significance of reducing friction cannot be overemphasized. This is especially true as oil reserves continue to decrease and energy costs are rising relentlessly. Most current lubricants contain petroleum base stocks, which are toxic to the environment and difficult to dispose of. Recently, due to environmental issues and increased regulations over contamination and pollution, there has been a growing concern on the use of mineral oils as lubricants. This concern has promoted a need for renewable and biodegradable lubricants. Currently, vegetable oils are being investigated as a potential source of environmentally favorable lubricants, due to a combination of biodegradability, renewability and excellent lubrication performance. Vegetable oils have enormous potential as alternatives and replacements for mineral oil in a myriad of industrial applications. However, one of the main disadvantages is their poor performance when working at high temperature and pressure. In the recent decade, there has been attention for the use of nanoparticles in many types of base ﬂuids. Nanoparticles have attracted considerable interest in recent years because of their excellent physical and chemical properties. However, inorganic nanoparticles very easily agglomerate in many mediums and have poor dispersive capacity in organic solvents and oil.

Intellectual Merit:
This project will be the first comprehensive study focused on the effect of nanoparticles with different characteristics (morphology, size) at different concentrations on the rheological behavior, thermophysical properties, and the tribological performance of vegetable oil-based nanolubricants. One of the main challenges will be to formulate stable suspensions because sediments and agglomerates will form over long period of the nanolubricants in stationary condition. Therefore, different surfactants and treatments will be used for the nanolubricants preparation. The fundamental understanding obtained will help to investigate the relation between the rheological behavior and thermophysical properties, on the tribological performance of the vegetable oil-based nanolubricants, and real applications. In addition, a model will be crated to predict the behavior based on nanoparticle characteristics, surfactant, concentrations, and type of vegetable oil.

Broader Impacts:
The broader impacts the proposed project may have are several and will significantly impact UTRGV transition towards an emerging research institution. If successful, this study will facilitate the fundamental understanding of characteristics that enable us to design and develop vegetable oil-based nanolubricants with superior tribological performance. Also, it will help to revitalize American manufacturing, to grow the national prosperity and workforce, and to reshape strategic industries. Most of the activities planned will be carried out by undergraduate and M.S. students. Specifically, the proposed project will strengthen existing courses as a result of this funding. In addition, one of the primary goals of The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) is to provide the opportunity of being engaged in high level research to as many undergraduate and graduate students as possible, as they pursue their degrees. With the training planned by the PI, undergraduate and graduate students will be capable of assisting in the development of new and novel products and the experimentation required for their characterization. The ability to contribute in a meaningful way to this level of science and engineering not only engages the student in the research but also has a direct and extremely positive impact on their retention, performance in their coursework, and their desire and ability to pursue graduate level education.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Faculty Seed Research Grant: Laser Surface Texturing based on FEA and CFD Simulations as an Innovative Technique for Addressing Multi-disciplinary Challenges in Engineering Applications
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: This study aims to utilize Laser Surface Texturing (LST) in combination with Finite Element Analysis (FEA) and Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations to improve the performance and longevity of important components in three distinct fields: prosthetic materials, rolling-element bearings, and airfoils. The goal is to enhance the quality of life and industrial performance by increasing the efficiency of prosthetic materials and rolling-element bearings. In airfoils, LST is being explored as a method to reduce drag and improve aerodynamic efficiency. The study involves applying LST to these components and then extensively evaluating the effects through experimentation and computational modeling. The FEA and CFD simulations will provide detailed insights into the performance of the LST-treated surfaces under various operating conditions. The findings of this research project are expected to have significant implications for biomedical engineering, materials science, mechanical engineering, and aeronautics, paving the way for future development and optimization.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Acquisition of Metal Additive Manufacturing Machine to Support Defense Manufacturing Research and Innovation at Rio Grande Valley and the National IDREAM4D Consortium
CONGRANT.SPONORG: DoD U.S. Army Contracting Command – Aberdeen Proving Ground – Research Triangle Park Division
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Groundbreaking advances in advanced manufacturing processes and smart technologies for cyber-physical systems are driving revolutions in materials/structures design and synthesis, providing innovation opportunities that transform a broader spectrum of military systems where advanced performance and protection at extreme conditions are expected. The objective of this request is to support a stream of ongoing research projects and two national consortia led by the PI team, through which 4 minority institutions are supported. Specifically, this requested major equipment supports UTRGV DoD Consortium for Innovation Driven Research Education for Advanced Manufacturing for the Defense (I-DREAM4D, www.idream4d.org) funded by DoD ($3.9 million, 2020-2024). The consortium is composed of five higher education institution members with three minority-serving institutions (UTRGV, UTSA, and Virginia State University), two national labs (Army Research Lab, Oak Ridge National Lab), members from defense industry, local high schools, and community colleges. The requested metal additive manufacturing machine facilitates the goals of the consortium to 1) advance research in material engineering through additive manufacturing (AM) and AI; 2) sustain an innovation-driven manufacturing education ecosystem to prepare future scientists and engineers who lead U.S. defense manufacturing innovation; and 3) expose and recruit future STEM talents through high school summer manufacturing innovation camps, and regional defense expos/exhibitions planned in 5 regions the consortium serves with a total population of 20 million, most of which are from underrepresented minority groups.
UTRVG, a multi-campus and the nation’s second-largest Hispanic-serving institute (HSI) has a record high total enrollment of 32,618 in Fall 2020, of whom 89.4% are Hispanic. The requested equipment is critical to the goal of increasing participation of underrepresented minorities in all STEM programs and specifically in advanced materials and manufacturing while broadening and enhancing UTRGV’s core priority of student success through engaged learning, research, and creative works that will transform the Rio Grande Valley, the Americas, and beyond.
The requested Metal Additive Manufacturing Equipment supports funded research projects and education programs organized in three levels, with the participation of minority students and faculty at UTRGV: 1) Advanced material synthesis and additive manufacturing science; 2) Materials/structure design enabled by AM and Artificial Intelligence (AI); and 3) Military devices and components enabled by AM and AI. Since 2019, the team has engaged more than 652 undergraduate students in the defense manufacturing education program, supported more than 95 students in funded research and industry projects, and exposed 1300 high school students to advanced defense manufacturing technologies though defense expos, summer camps, and invited talks provided by DoD. The team at UTRGV was recenlty selected by DOE/NNSA and NSF for awards of two large grants ($9 million total) to prepare STEM talents and to advance research at UTRGV, leveraging AM for energy production and critical infrastructures. Currently, the team only has limited access to a Renishaw AM 400 machine located in LA, California, through a collaboration arrangement, which is no longer sufficient to support the research and education programs at UTRGV. The pandemic has additionally caused serious logistic challenges to all operations at every facet. Direct access to modern metal additive manufacturing machines is in desperate need to support a stream of funded projects, support student learning in STEM, and support impactful outreach programs the team offers.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of a Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) for Advanced Materials Research and Education Programs at the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
PROJECT SUMMARY

Overview:
The objective of the present MRI proposal is to acquire a state-of-the-art Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) that will support interdisciplinary research and education programs at UTRGV. The STEM combines the principles of transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. The proposed instrument (Talos™ F200i) is flexible and compact 200 kV Field Emission Gun (FEG) STEM, designed for precise and quantitative characterization of nanomaterials and biological cells. It combines an outstanding quality in high-resolution STEM imaging with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS). In addition, the instrument is equipped with tomographic capabilities via software for alignment of a tomographic series of images, and 3D reconstruction of the data.

Intellectual Merit:
The acquisition of the Talos™ F200i STEM instrument will enable a significant enhancement of basic research toolset across a wide range of materials, medical education and research programs including Chemistry, Physics, Medicine and Mechanical, Electrical and Manufacturing Engineering at UTRGV. Specifically, the proposed equipment will support projects to advance the development and characterization of different nanoparticles as lubricant additives, composite nanofibers, high entropy alloys (HEA) prepared by Selective Laser Melting technology, regenerative medicine, polymers, and nanomaterials for use in , patterned magnetic arrays, temperature controlled drug delivery systems, bioimaging, nanostructured energetic devices, semiconductors, high temperature superconductors, and radiation induced functional materials. The acquisition of the STEM will broaden the research scope for all participants, making it possible to address new scientific challenges in new transformative research directions.

Broader Impacts:
This proposal brings together a diverse group of faculty members and will significantly impact UTRGV transition towards an emerging research institution. In addition, most of the projects will be carried out by undergraduate and M.S. students. Specifically, the instrument will strengthen existing courses and several more will be developed as a result of this funding. Additionally, it will significantly support research and education programs operated at the DoD I-DREAM4D Consortium, which was recently funded by DoD on a $4 million grant and NSF PREM funded projects. It can also be integrated in the K12 outreach and education efforts organized by the colleges and the consortium at national scale. Results from the research projects supported by this instrument will be disseminated in peer journal articles and national/international conferences to stimulate further understanding and progress of the various research areas of the investigators discussed in this proposal. More importantly, this proposal will:1) Promote a hands-on, entrepreneurial, educational experience, and training of graduate and undergraduate students in advanced materials, nanomaterial design, biomaterials and characterization; 2) Enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV; 3) Enhance the interdisciplinary research partnership between different departments at UTRGV to better compete for external funding; and 4) Increase the Hispanic Student retention rate at UTRGV

In summary, the Talos™ F200i instrument acquisition will strengthen the existing materials and medical research infrastructure at UTRGV and enhance the research and educational experiences of many students at UTRGV and South Texas region.

CONGRANT.TITLE: DoD-HBCUMI Equipment: Acquisition of Metal Additive Manufacturing Machine to Support Defense Manufacturing Research and Innovation at Rio Grande Valley and the National I-DREAM4D Consortium
DoD-HBCUMI Equipment: Acquisition of an Advanced Materials’ Surface Characterization System for Science and Engineering Research and Education at South Texas
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The objective of this proposal is to acquire a state of the art surface characterization system including nano-indentation, micro-indentation, micro-scratch tester, and AFM that will support multidisciplinary research projects and education programs in areas of interest to DoD at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV). The proposed system will include cutting-edge features needed to characterize a broad range of materials and provide the capability to investigate mechanical, tribological and other physical properties at nanostructured scales for materials that are too thin to be tested using conventional methods. In addition, UTRGV has in place a magnetron sputtering system (AJA International, A300) for research in physical vapor deposition (PVD). The acquisition of the proposed equipment will allow the surface characterization of the materials created by the sputtering system, which will immediately benefit research and educational projects in areas of interest to DoD. These projects include the following: (1) High temperature characterization of novel thermal barrier coatings created by PVD. Encompassing the development of novel PVD protective thermal barrier coatings TBC for gas turbine engines and the analytical methods to study their mechanical properties and adhesion to turbine blade materials at elevated temperatures. (2) Cost-effective CIGS thin films for novel solar power technology, encompassing the development of thin film solar cell like Copper Indium Gallium Di-Selenide (CIGS) with an optimized design considering the efficiency and cost effectiveness, to be used for space and satellite applications. Further, theoretical and numerical models will be developed, and the simulated result will be compared with experimental data. (3) Investigation of additive synthesis of intermetallic (IM) containing high entropy alloys (HEAs) directly from pure elemental powders using multiple metal additive manufacturing processes. Research in HEAs will open a nearly infinite space for novel engineering materials with trans-scale structures delivering superior properties required in extreme conditions normally expected in many defense systems. (4) Biointerfacing of functional nanofilaments for health/biothreat monitoring and life research. This project aims for the development of a novel functional system: Biohazard and Radiation Sensing (BRS). Integrated functional materials (IFM) will be grafted onto functional metal oxide with an immediate successive mesoporous micro layer surrounded by composite oxides. Advanced integrated materials systems with an innovative embedded BRS sensor system for real-time monitoring of biological and radiation hazards will be developed. (5) High energy density nanostructured composites with tailored particles size and shapes. The development of novel nanoenergetic materials, their design, synthesis and fabrication procedures are critical for national security and it was recognized as a significant addition to support advanced military formulations. The goal of this project is to explore the physics-based knowledge in energy release, shock waves and pressure discharge needed to enhance the performance and functionality of novel high density nanoenergetic composites with tailored particle shapes and size to reduce the mass and volume of munitions systems and components. The instrument will form a nucleus for a broad collaboration of scholars, resulting in further funding opportunities.  Additionally, the proposed equipment will facilitate efforts at UTRGV to reach out to traditionally underrepresented groups within science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields. The opportunity to participate in a state-of-the-art research projects motivates UTRGV students from a diverse background to pursue graduate school (M.S. or Ph.D. degrees). Furthermore, the acquisition of the proposed equipment will support development of physics, materials science, and engineering doctoral programs. Lastly, the proposed equipment will support the educational programs developed by the consortium for Innovation Driven Research/Education Ecosystem for Advanced Manufacturing for the Defense (I-DREAM4D) directed by Dr. J. Li at UTRGV.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of a single crystal/powder X-ray diffractometer
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The objective of this grant application is to acquire a cutting-edge single crystal/powder X-ray diffractometer SC-XRD/PXRD to support fundamental and interdisciplinary research projects and the education program in the South Texas region. The instrument will be installed at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and will support to a broad range of users and will be used as shared instrumentation. The goal of this acquisition is to enable the following: (i) Pursue new research avenues; (ii) Advance current research programs; and (iii) Enhance pedagogical techniques and enrich training in the undergraduate and graduate programs in STEM field.
The X-ray diffractometer system will buttress the development of advanced materials at UTRGV in an array of applications, including, but not limited to, electrocatalysis, lithium-ion batteries, molecular catalysis, and ferromagnetic materials. These diverse research thrusts would be substantially aided by state-of-the-art X-ray diffraction with overarching applications in sensors, energy storage, environmental sustainability, protein characterization, organic methodology, and disease diagnosis/treatment. The single crystal X-ray diffractometer allows for the unambiguous determination of the solid-state structure of molecular materials including accurate data on the 3D spatial arrangements of atoms, molecules, the interatomic distance between atoms, bond angles and neighboring atoms.
UTRGV is a Hispanic Serving Institution located in South Texas and has the largest Hispanic student population (~90%) in Texas. Individuals from Hispanic ethnicity are historically underrepresented in the STEM workforce and in higher education STEM-disciplines. Faculty members spanning several departments at UTRGV will directly use the requested system for their existing and new research projects as well as the training of highly qualified personnel. Graduate and undergraduate students are expected to take on a leadership role in the proposed interdisciplinary research projects. The acquisition of the X-ray diffractometer will enhance existing outreach efforts with local High school students and teachers during the UTRGV’s summer design camp administered by the research team of this MRI proposal. These integrated activities will unequivocally strengthen research, education, and student participation across programs in chemistry, biology, physics and engineering at UTRGV. In addition, the SC-XRD system will become a tool to bolster regional collaboration of universities and community colleges in South Texas. The personnel exposed to the SC-XRD prioritize fostering an environment of equity and inclusion for underrepresented minority students.

Intellectual Merit: The SC-XRD instrument acquisition will enable significant enhancement of basic
research toolset across a wide range of materials characterization including but not limited to molecular catalysts, nanomaterials, stimuli-responsive assemblies, supramolecular materials, biological materials, and gas sensors. Determination of molecular structure allows for furthering fundamental understanding of structure-function studies in the interdisciplinary research thrusts in this proposal. Characterization of molecular materials ranging in size from well-defined small molecules to more complex biological systems and solid-state materials is a prerequisite to advance the knowledge of broad research directions at UTRGV.

Broader Impacts: The acquisition of the X-ray diffractometer will advance research at UTRGV in the broadly defined areas of materials and biomaterials. The X-ray diffractometer will also enhance the research/educational experience of undergraduate and graduate students at UTRGV from a wide array of science and engineering disciplines. Both the SC-XRD and PXRD will be heavily featured in course curriculum currently offered in the Chemistry, Engineering, and Physics department at UTRGV. The SC-XRD functionality specifically, will foster a research hub in the south-Texas region and bolster collaborative work between researchers at UTRGV and other schools in south Texas including Texas A&M Corpus Christi, Texas A&M Kingsville, and Texas A&M International University. Collaborative efforts between these HSI’s in the south Texas region, will enhance the participation and training of under-represented students in STEM-based disciplines. Continued efforts in outreach to local high schools and community colleges will be enhanced and further recruitment and preparation of local underrepresented populations. The team will ensure that inclusion of women and underrepresented minority students are prioritized in research and educational activities.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Proposal to Establish a National Center for Integrated Transportation Infrastructure 4.0: Improving the Durability and Extending the Life of Transportation Infrastructure
CONGRANT.SPONORG: U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT) UTC Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
This proposal establishes the Center for Integrated Transportation Infrastructure 4.0 (CITI-4.0), a National University Transportation Center focusing on “Improving the Durability and Extending the Life of Transportation Infrastructure”. CITI 4.0 is a consortium of seven US higher education and research institutions that consolidate their expertise, facilities, resources, and institutional support to achieve the common goals of the center. The center addresses the challenges of the new era Intelligent Transportation System in ways never previously imagined by adapting the “Industry 4.0” principles to the integrated transportation infrastructure. CITI-4.0 introduces automation, cyber-physical fusion and information driven practices, enabled by real-time data communications among heterogeneous monitoring sensors and integrates the assessment, management and maintenance activities of the infrastructure, resources and operations across railways, roadways, and ports following a data-driven performance-based approach.

Motives: North America’s demand for safe, affordable, and environmentally responsible transportation of people and goods by railway, roadway, and ports is projected to grow substantially in the years ahead. Asset managers are consistently challenged to improve the performance of the transportation network, optimize efficiency of operations and ensure safety by maximizing accessibility and reliability of the transportation infrastructure. Although accurate monitoring is a key enabler for effective operations and maintenance, the condition assessment is currently conducted based mainly on periodic, labor-intensive and time-consuming scheduled activities. The interpretation of the collected data and integration with operations is extensively dependent on the experience of the operators and other human factors. Each transportation mode relies typically on its own operations, infrastructure, and resources to meet the current network demand. These three elements are often loosely integrated within each mode, are rarely integrated across modes, and are not effectively engaged with the end users of the network.

Topic Areas: The center activities cover the following non-exclusive topics: (1) Application of new materials and technologies; (2) Cyber and communications security; (3) Condition monitoring, remote sensing, and the use of GPS; (4) Asset and performance management through data accessibility, data security and analytical tools;

Impacts: CITI-4.0 brings the infrastructure of the major transportation modes into the Industry 4.0 era as essential parts of the grand Intelligent Transportation System. The proposed CITI-4.0 research, education, workforce development, technology transfer, and diversity activities advance technology in transportation engineering and enable students and professionals from diverse socioeconomic groups throughout the country to develop the skills necessary to overcome the transportation challenges of the next era and create the next generation of worldwide leaders. This initiative benefits all stakeholders in the transportation industry, administration and legislation and sets the framework for addressing similar problems around the world.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Cost and energy savings in industrial activities across the US-Mexico border through environmentally friendly vegetable-oil based nano-lubricants
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The present innovative collaborative research project comprises a joint effort between The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) and Universidad de Monterrey (UDEM) to develop and evaluate new environmentally friendly vegetable-oil based nano-lubricants to support industrial activities across the US-Mexico border and promote energy savings specifically in the metal-mechanic industry. According to new studies, about 23% of the world´s energy consumption is spent to overcome friction between moving components and to replace or repair worn tooling and materials.  In the context of energy efficiency, the significance of reducing friction cannot be overemphasized. This is especially true as oil reserves continue to decrease and energy costs are rising relentlessly. Most current lubricants contain petroleum base stocks, which are toxic to environment and difficult to dispose of after use. Recently, due to environmental issues and growing regulations over contamination and pollution there has been a growing concern on the use of mineral oils as lubricants. This concern has promoted a need for renewable and biodegradable lubricants. Since we live on a planet with finite resources, we must think about the future generations and work for a sustainable development in the field of tribology. Currently, vegetable oils are being investigated as a potential source of environmentally favorable lubricants, due to a combination of biodegradability, renewability and excellent lubrication performance. Based on common research interests, the main aim of the present collaborative research project is to develop new vegetable-oil based nano-lubricants by combining vegetable oils available in Texas and Mexico and environmentally friendly nanoclays. If awarded, the ConTEX collaborative research project will promote a strong collaboration between faculty and students form UTRGV and UDEM and will act as a vehicle to expose more engineering students to scientific research, to provide them with more opportunities to publish in scientific journals and present their work at symposiums, as well as to better prepare them to enter the STEM workforce and/or encourage them to pursue advanced degrees.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The objective of this proposed project is 1) to develop super-hard [1] metal/ceramic compounds (hardness in the range of 40-80 GPa) with multiscale structures and tailored properties in the full 3D space, leveraging a novel high throughput laser additive alloying (LAA) process that 3D forms super-hard high configurational entropy alloy (HEAs) borides compounds directly from multiple principal elements, and 2) to investigate computational methods for quick prediction of materials-processes-properties relationships to efficiently explore and synthesis ultra-hard composites (hardness above 80 GPa) by incorporating ultra-hard nanoparticles such as nano-diamond [2] and boron nitride in the matrix of in-situ formed HEAs.

CONGRANT.TITLE: NSF MRI: Acquisition of a Surface Characterization Platform for Surface Engineering/Materials Research and Education Programs at the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The objective of this Major Research Instrumentation (MRI) proposal is to acquire a cutting-edge mechanical surface characterization platform including nanoindentation, micro-indentation, micro-scratch tester, and AFM that will support multidisciplinary research and education programs at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV).
Nanoindentation is used to probe the mechanical properties of materials at the nano-size scale (approximately 10-7 to 10-9 meters). The system will include features needed to characterize a broad range of materials such as nanocrystalline alloys, polymer nanocomposite films, thin hard films, semiconductors, and conducting films from metallic nanoparticle dispersion precursors. The mechanical surface characterization platform will provide critical information about the behavior of materials for a variety of scientific and engineering challenges. It will create new opportunities to integrate research, education, training, and outreach. The capability to probe mechanical properties at nano-size scales is required for films that are too thin to test using conventional methods and for other materials whose properties are engineered by manipulating their structure at these small length scales. In addition, UTRGV has in place a magnetron sputtering system (AJA International, A300) for research in physical vapor deposition (PVD). The system is capable to create thin PVD ceramic films for different research areas. The acquisition of the mechanical surface characterization platform will immediately benefit research and educational projects in engineering, materials science, chemistry and physics at UTRGV.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Laser surface texturing technology to decrease the energy consumption and improve the performance of transportation infrastructure roller bearings
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The objective of the present research project is to investigate the use of a new technology of laser surface texturing to improve the performance, durability, and decrease the energy consumption of transportation infrastructure bearings. The growing emphasis on cost-effectiveness and energy-efficiency has significantly resulted in elevating adoption of bearings across varied application areas. These applications include roadways (e.g. agriculture, industrial, automotive, mining, and construction), railways and ports. The proposed study will include the surface modification of cylindrical-roller bearing components through laser surface texturing (LST) technology and the experimental and numerical acquisition of bearing operational data as a function of load, speed, time, ambient temperature, and bearing condition. The bearing operational data to be collected include operational temperature, vibration signals, and energy consumption (current). Also, the tribological behavior, including coefficient of friction (COF) and wear, of different LST patterns will be evaluated trough tribological tests using block-on-ring configuration. Collaborators have already developed a thermal finite element model that can simulate some normal and abnormal bearing operating conditions. Using experimental results, the PI’s will study the correlation between tribological behavior and operating conditions of different LST patterns on cylindrical-roller bearings. The developed correlation can then be used to determine the impact of laser surface texturing to maximize the bearing durability. It will also provide the opportunity to use the enhanced operating conditions while the texturizing lasts to estimate the life remaining in the bearing components. In addition, the developed correlation provides insight into possible areas of improvement for the next generation of transportation infrastructure bearings with improved performance and extended life.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Development, Characterization, and Modeling of Multi-Layer Fabric Reinforced with Shear-Thickening Fluids Created with Sub-Micron Silica and Soda-Lime Glass Particles
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Researchers at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley (UTRGV) have developed patent pending technologies to convert waste glass into single-digit micron and sub-micron (300±200 nanometers) glass particles that have unique properties not found in bulk glass. Waste glass is typical soda lime glass with about 60-90% silica and 40-10% other (sodium, calcium, and aluminum) oxides. The principal investigators (PIs) at UTRGV have found that the properties of recycled glass fine particles that have been processed into superfine particles are dramatically different. The PIs are interested in understanding the myriad of processing-property-microstructure relationships of these glass particles and composites (i.e., multi-layer fabric reinforced with shear thickening fluids made from these particles). The basic science research component of this DoD project will initially concentrate on submicron silica or glass particles by themselves to define and demonstrate systematically the underlying processing-property-microstructure relationships, and their controlled manipulation under dynamic conditions to create the next generation composites for superior performance. Modeling efforts will include experimentally informed and validated finite element analysis. After gaining a thorough insight into each type of particle, the study will be extended to the combination of micron and submicron silica and glass particles. The soda-lime glass fine particles can be commercially produced from waste glass for under a dollar (target price) a pound, which also has a positive impact on the environment through recycling. Equally relevant is the fact that it is foreseen that these submicron glass particles can be produced in commercial quantities of tens of tons per day. These new materials and derived material systems and their properties have a great potential to address key Department of Defense, ARMY Research Office (ARO) interests. Specifically, (a) detailed understanding of complex material system behavior and its capability during service, and (b) to utilize material’s capabilities close to their limiting capacity (ARO, Solid Mechanics - Understanding of Mechanical Behavior of Complex Material Systems). In order to further motivate, inspire, and engage STEM students at UTRGV, additional educational/outreach activities will include a number of focused DoD applied research projects that are linked with the basic science research, which will attract and actively engage undergraduate senior design groups. Relating to the ARO Mechanical Behavior of Materials, the aim of body armor applied research is to develop a low cost, lightweight, wearable garment system with ballistic impact resistance which is very amenable to our basic research. In addition, all research/educational results will be published in journals and conferences and presented to the rest of the student body at UTRGV at professional symposiums and poster presentations highlighting DoD opportunities for student professional development. It is important to note that the PIs have all the necessary facilities and equipment (including a new state-of-the-art oven with programmable and controlled environment including vacuum and inert gases) to perform the proposed basic and applied research. Some of the equipment has been designed and fabricated here at UTRGV by our undergraduate students under the supervision of the PIs.

NSF IUSE HSI Implementation and Evaluation Project: The Freshman Year Innovator Experience (FYIE): Bridging the URM Gap in STEM.
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The University of X's Freshman Year Innovator Experience (FYIE) program, hosted at a Minority Serving Institution (MSI), seeks to improve the first-year experience for new students by nurturing essential academic success skills. Specifically tailored to freshman mechanical engineering students, the program aims to equip them with self-transformation skills to navigate through the amplified academic and professional obstacles brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic. Participants of FYIE engage in two concurrent courses: Introduction to Engineering (Course A) and Learning Frameworks (Course B). In Course A, students undertake a 6-week engineering design project, while in Course B, they work on a 6-week academic career path project. Throughout these simultaneous projects, time-bound interventions highlight the similarities between the engineering design process and the academic career pathways project. The main goal is for students to recognize that the design thinking skills acquired in the engineering design process can be applied to resolve their academic career challenges. The FYIE program was initiated as a pilot in the spring semester of 2023, with instructors from Course A and B introducing the parallel projects. The implementation has continued through the fall 2023, spring 2024, and ongoing fall 2024 semesters, introducing improvements at every iteration, with adjustments made to the parallel projects and the identification of intervention points for self-transformation through analogy. The creators of the program will present the outcomes from the pilot implementations and address the obstacles and future work. This proposed endeavor is aligned with the continuous mission of the College of Engineering and Computer Science (CECS) at the University of X, which includes: 1) increasing the number of STEM degrees granted to Hispanics, 2) promoting the participation of women in STEM-related fields, and 3) enhancing persistence and self-confidence in STEM fields amidst the challenges posed by COVID-19. The project is supported by the NSF award 2225247.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Work in Progress: Development of A Boostcamp for Freshman Student Success During COVID-19 Transition
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Assessment results show that passing rates in introductory courses and retention rates of first-year students in the College of Engineering and Computer Science at The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, a predominantly Hispanic Serving Institution (HSI), significantly dropped with the onset of COVID-19. These results and trends highlight the academic preparation of incoming students, particularly the new cohort of underrepresented Hispanic students from underserved and challenged communities in the region, who may not have sufficiently develop the necessary skills (e.g., adaptability, persistence, and performance) for the rigor of engineering education. To address this challenge, an onboarding “boostcamp” was created for incoming and transfer students to bridge the transition from secondary education to higher education. The boostcamp primes students to overcome academic deficiencies, develop a critical skills portfolio, learn problem-solving techniques, build a sustainable community of mentoring support with faculty and students, and gain a template to sustain academic and professional success during their undergraduate education. The paper presents the boostcamp's design process steps, including curricular analysis, identification of areas for improvement, skills inventory, and blueprinting, as well as its initial implementation in the mechanical engineering program. The boostcamp was organized over a week and featured hands-on engineering activities, faculty and student talks, and engineering lab tours. It was based on a design thinking approach and structured around Challenge-based Instruction, innovation, design, and mentoring. Daily activities focused on promoting critical thinking, assertiveness in the face of adversity, informed decision-making, and task prioritization. Results indicate that the boostcamp increased student confidence and established a valuable network system among participants. Future work will focus on expanding the boostcamp to include students from other engineering and computer science departments and developing a template for other institutions with similar challenges.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Work in Progress: Teaching Engineering Students to Self-Transform: Parallelisms between Product Innovation and Student Career Path Planning
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Freshman engineering students can have a hard time transitioning to college. The freshman year is critical to the students’ academic success; in this year they learn basic skills and establish essential networks with other students, faculty, and resources. How can we help these freshman engineering students in this transition? We propose that freshman students can learn from the engineering design innovation process and apply it by analogy to the design of their academic pathways. There are multiple similarities between product innovation (i.e., technology) and the continuous academic challenges faced by the student. Engineers as designers and innovators have a vast and rich repository of techniques, tools, and approaches to develop new technologies, and a parallelism can be drawn between the design and innovation of a technology (e.g., redesign of a kitchen appliance), and the “design” of the students’ academic career pathways. During the Spring 2023 semester pilot, students in Intro to Mechanical Engineering (Course A) worked in teams in a 6-week product innovation project to redesign a simple kitchen appliance. Students learned basic concepts of the design process (e.g., creative exploration of solutions, decision making, multi objective evaluation, etc.). These same students concurrently took Course B (Learning Frameworks) where they worked on a 6-week project to define their career pathways. Both projects, product innovation and career pathways, followed the Challenge Based Instruction (CBI) approach. Periodically, participant students were shown how to use the lessons from product innovation by analogy and reflection in their career pathways project. The objective is for students to learn about the engineering design process and to apply it to their academic challenges by analogy. This prepares students with meta skills to help solve future problems in their academic path, and at each iteration, the students transform themselves, hence the use of the term self-transformation (also referred as “self-innovation”). Data collected from pre and post surveys will be presented to measure self-efficacy in engineering design, grit, motivation to learn, and STEM identity. Participant interviews provide a qualitative insight into the intervention. This project is funded by NSF award 2225247.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Study on the Tribological Properties of DIN 16MnCr5 Steel after Duplex Gas-Nitriding and Pack Boriding
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: DIN 16MnCr5 is commonly used in mechanical engineering contact applications such as gears, joint parts, shafts, gear wheels, camshafts, bolts, pins, and cardan joints, among others. This study examined the microstructural and mechanical properties and tribological behavior of different surface treatments applied to DIN 16MnCr5 steel. The samples were hardened at 870 °C for 15 min and then quenched in water. The surface conditions evaluated were as follows: quenched and tempered DIN 16MnCr5 steel samples without surface treatments (control group), quenched and tempered DIN 16MnCr5 steel samples with gas-nitriding at 560 °C for 6 h, quenched and tempered DIN 16MnCr5 steel samples with pack boriding at 950 °C for 4 h, and quenched and tempered DIN 16MnCr5 steel samples with duplex gas-nitriding and pack boriding. Microstructure characterization was carried out using metallographic techniques, optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy with energy-dispersive spectroscopy, and X-ray diffraction. The mechanical properties were assessed through microhardness and elastic modulus tests using nanoindentation. The tribological behavior was evaluated using pin-on-disc tests following the ASTM G99-17 standard procedure under dry sliding conditions. The results indicated that the surface treated with duplex gas-nitriding and pack boriding exhibited the highest wear resistance and a reduced coefficient of friction due to improved mechanical properties, leading to increased hardness and elastic modulus.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Characterization of Microstructural and Mechanical Properties of 17-4 PH Stainless Steel by Cold Rolled and Machining vs. DMLS Additive Manufacturing
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Journal of Manufacturing and Materials Processing
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The 17-4 PH stainless steel is widely used in the aerospace, petrochemical, chemical, food, and general metallurgical industries. The present study was conducted to analyze the mechanical properties of two types of 17-4 PH stainless steel—commercial cold-rolled and direct metal laser sintering (DMLS) manufactured. This study employed linear and nonlinear tensile FEM simulations, combined with various materials characterization techniques such as tensile testing and nanoindentation. Moreover, microstructural analysis was performed using metallographic techniques, optical microscopy, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS), and X-ray diffraction (XRD). The results on the microstructure for 17-4 PH DMLS stainless steel reveal the layers of melting due to the laser process characterized by complex directional columnar structures parallel to the DMLS build direction. The mechanical properties obtained from the simple tension test decreased by 17% for the elastic modulus, 7.8% for the yield strength, and 7% for the ultimate strength for 17-4 PH DMLS compared with rolled 17-4 PH stainless steel. The FEM simulation using the experimental tension test data revealed that the 17-4 PH DMLS stainless steel experienced a decrease in the yield strength of ~8% and in the ultimate strength of ~11%. A reduction of the yield strength of the material was obtained as the grain size increased.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Assessing the Lubrication Performance of Sunflower Oil Modified With Montmorillonite Clay (MMT) Nanoparticles for Industrial Applications

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: ASME International Mechanical Engineering Congress and Exposition, Proceedings (IMECE)
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Because of the environmental impact and price volatility, there has been a growing concern about using petroleum-based lubricants. This issue has encouraged research into the development of biodegradable lubricants like vegetable oils. This study assessed the tribological behavior of sunflower oil modified with Montmorillonite nanoclay (MMT) as lubricant additives. A block-on-ring tribometer was used to assess the wear and friction characteristics of the nano-lubricants. A custom-made tapping torque tester was used to evaluate the nano-lubricants in a real-world application. It was found that the volumetric wear, Coefficient of Friction, and torque of the system decreased when MMT nanoparticles were added. The experimental results indicated that sunflower oil modified with 2.0 wt.% MMT exhibited the best tribological behavior, reducing COF and wear volume loss by 88% and 63%, respectively. Based on the results, the newly developed sunflower oil-based nano-lubricants, with the addition of MMT nanoclay, could be a promising environmentally friendly solution to compete with petroleum-based lubricants.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: In the present research project, a novel portable battery-powered handheld device able to produce micron and submicron fibers using centrifugal forces is proposed. The design includes spinnerets with a clamshell configuration with multiple chambers or reservoirs (2, 4, and 8) and different exit orifice diameters (400, 500, 600, and 800 µm). The rotational speed is controlled via an Arduino microcontroller. To validate the design, a series of experiments were conducted and the effect of orifices diameter, number of chambers, and velocity on the resulting fibers diameter and yield was studied. For the experiments, a polymeric solution of Polyvinyl Alcohol (PVA) was prepared. The fiber yield was gravimetrically quantified, and the fiber morphology and diameter were analyzed by means of scanning electron microscopy (SEM). The experimental results showed that spinnerets with an orifice diameter of 500 microns yielded the greatest amount of fibers (0.0777 grams). In addition, the number of chambers also affected the amount of fibers produced, and it was determined that the fiber diameter size is dependent on spinneret speed. Fibers with 80 nm in diameter were observed at 6500 rpm.

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: A modular torque measuring instrument capable of performing tapping torque tests (TTT) according to the ASTM D-5619 standard was designed, developed, and validated. With this new instrument, the performance of different lubricants can be evaluated in terms of frictional torque and energy consumption during tapping processes. This instrument can adapt onto any conventional milling machine or CNC machine and operate under various machining operations such as tapping, drilling, and other processes. To validate the design and performance of this new device, three commercially available lubricants were evaluated. From the three tested conditions, the results showed good repeatability, with consistent results throughout the different tests for each lubricant. The impact of such a proposed instrument ranges from academic use to industrial business use.

Multidirectional Pin-on-Disk Testing Device to Evaluate the Cross-shear Effect on the Wear of Biocompatible Materials
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: One of the main causes of hip prostheses failure is the premature wear of their components. Multi-directional motion or “cross-shear” motion has been identified as one of the most significant factors affecting the wear rate of UHMWPE in total hip joint replacement prostheses. To better evaluate the effect of this cross-shear motion on the tribological behavior of different biomaterials, a new wear testing device has been designed and developed. This new instrument is capable to reproduce the “cross-shear” effect with bidirectional motion on bearing materials and to determine coefficient of friction (COF) between surfaces during testing. To validate the functionality of this new testing platform, alumina balls were articulated against Ti-6Al-4V ELI alloy disks in Ringer’s solution. Four different articulation patterns, all with identical path lengths per cycle, were tested. Gravimetric weight loss was converted to volumetric wear data in order to determine the effects of motion patterns on the wear. Worn surfaces were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy. This scientific approach to quantifying the tribological effects of cross-shear provides fundamental data that are crucial in evaluating potential biomaterials for use in knee and hip joint replacements.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Biotribological study of multi-nano-layers as a coating for total hip prostheses
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Metal-on-metal (MOM) hip joint bearings have demonstrated low wear rates. However, wear of MOM joints is a concern due to the toxicity and biological reaction of wear debris and dissolution by metallic corrosion. There is, therefore, considerable interest in further reducing the wear of MOM bearings for hip prostheses. The aim of the present study was to investigate the wear properties of surface engineered CoCr cast metal-on-metal hip prostheses. For this purpose, a nano-layer coating system (TiN/CrN)×25≈1µm was prepared by physical vapor deposition (PVD) for the femoral heads. On the other hand, the acetabular cups were treated by PVD obtaining a coating of CrN≈4µm. The femoral heads were tested against the acetabular cups using a three-axial multi-station hip joint simulator. During the wear tests three directions of motion were applied with the following amplitudes: flexion–extension (FE) ±23°, abduction–adduction (AA) ±23° and internal–external rotation (IER) ±8°. All components were undertaken at 1.2Hz under a single axis loading pattern with a maximum load peak of 2kN and bovine calf serum solution as lubricant. Surface damage analysis performed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy disperse spectroscopy (EDS) showed the wear mechanisms involved during wear tests. Mild adhesion and delamination between the multilayers of contact sections of the surface were evidenced. However, at 2 million cycles, the metal matrix was not worn resulting in a significant improvement of the wear resistance.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Micro-Abrasive Wear Testing of Surface Engineered Surgical Grade CoCrMo Alloy for Biotribological Applications
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Wear of metal-on-metal hip joints is a concern due to the toxicity and biological reaction of wear debris. Retrieved CoCrMo hip implants have shown that abrasive wear is the predominant failure mechanism in such joints. There have been some efforts to improve the wear resistance of joint implants through the application of hard biocompatible ceramic coatings. However, the adhesion of the coatings has been a concern. The aim of the present work was to study the wear resistance of surface engineered CoCrMo alloy intended for biotribological applications by means of an abrasive wear test, based on the ball-crater technique. Different surface conditions were obtained on surgical grade wrought CoCrMo alloy: plasma nitrided, physical vapor deposition (PVD) coated (monolayer CrN and multilayer (TiN/CrN)x3) and modified using duplex surface engineering technology (a combination of the two previous approaches: plasma nitriding followed by plasma assisted PVD). The engineered surfaces were characterized by scanning electron microscopy, nanoindentation and, atomic force microscopy (AFM). Scratch test was used to determine the influence of the duplex technology on the adhesion of the coatings to substrate. The wear resistance of the different surface conditions was determined using a slurry abrasive micro-abrasion testing device. It was found that the duplex engineering technology enables a significant rise in the resistance of surfaces against concentrated loading modes, improving the adhesion of the coatings to the substrate; however, it has no significant influence improving the wear resistance of the samples during the abrasive wear tests.

PRESENT.TITLE: Characterization of vegetable oil-based lubricants with Halloysite Nanotubes as lubricant additives and their tribological performance
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Vegetable oil-based nano-lubricants are a great alternative to petroleum-based lubricants due to their less adverse impact on the environment. This work evaluated the tribological performance of sunflower, corn, and peanut oils with the addition of Halloysite Nanotubes (HNT) as lubricant additives at different concentrations. Vegetable oils are commercially used as edible oils, but in this current work they were selected as base oils for the nano-lubricants due to their renewability and biodegradability. To analyze the tribology performance of the nano-lubricants, a block-on-ring tribometer was used following the ASTM G-077-05 standard procedure. In addition, tapping torque tests were carried out following the ASTM D5619 standard. Results indicated that sunflower, corn, and peanut oils mixed with HNT at 1.5 wt% provided the best tribological performance. The wear volume loss was lowered by 29%, 78%, and 67% for sunflower, corn, and peanut oil respectively, with the addition of 1.5 wt%, compared to its base oil. Tapping torque test results also provided high tapping torque efficiency that can prolong tool life in machining processes. Based on the experimental results, it can be concluded that the vegetable oils modified with the addition of halloysite nano-clay have the potential to be used as biodegradable lubricants.

PRESENT.NAME: 16th North American Conference on Industrial Engineering and Operations Management
PRESENT.TITLE: Development of Vegetable Oil-based Nano-lubricants using MMT Nanoparticles as Lubricant Additives
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Because of the environmental impact and price volatility, there has been a growing concern on the use of petroleum-based lubricants. This issue has stimulated research into the development of biodegradable lubricants like vegetable oils. In this study, the tribological and rheological behavior of sunflower, peanut, and corn oils modified with montmorillonite nanoclay (MMT) as lubricant additives were evaluated at various concentrations. A custom-made block on ring tribotester was used to evaluate the wear and friction characteristics of the nano-lubricants, following the ASTM G-077-05 standard. The effects of concentration and shear rate on shear viscosity were studied using a parallel plate rheometer, and the experimental data was compared with conventional models. Analytical methods, including scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-Ray diffraction (XRD), thermogravimetric analysis (TGA), and profilometry, were used to characterize the morphology and structure of the MMT nanoclay, as well as the worn surfaces. The experimental results showed that the volumetric wear and coefficient of friction decreased with the addition of MMT nanoparticles, at different concentrations, compared to the base vegetable oils. In conclusion, the newly developed vegetable oil-based nano-lubricants with the addition of MMT nanoclay, look like a promising environmentally friendly solution to compete with petroleum-based lubricants.

PRESENT.TITLE: Development and Characterization of Cold Spray Coatings for Aerospace and Defense Manufacturing
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Cold Spray is a type of thermal metal spraying which uses heated gas/air to propel metal powder onto the surface of a substrate to create a coating or repair damaged or corroded metal components. The powder feedstock materials are spherical gas atomized metal powders ranging in size from 20-50 microns in diameter for best results. Cold spray systems use low temperatures ranging from 200-900 °C compared to existing additive manufacturing methods which use much higher temperatures to melt metal. These lower heating temperatures only semi-melt the metal powder particles allowing for them to undergo plastic deformation as they are deposited onto the surface of the substrate. The main objective of this project is to develop and characterize cold spray coatings using aluminum, copper, and nickel powders deposited on different substrates varying processing parameters. As cold spray can be used in different coating applications with a wide range of different metals and alloys, coatings have an unlimited range in applications where rapid repair and high-quality coatings are needed. The ease of use of this technology has a promising future in aerospace and defense applications as it provides a low-cost solution in corrosion prevention and repair of damaged components.

PRESENT.ABSTRACT:
COVID-19 was declared a pandemic by the World Health Organization on 11 March 2020. The transmission of COVID-19 occurs through cough or respiratory droplets, bodily fluids, and contaminated surfaces. Facemasks have become a worldwide healthcare necessity for the COVID-19 pandemic to ensure health in our communities.
The first goal is to design and develop a lightweight, comfortable, and secure 3D printed facemask. This will be done by experimenting with different material combinations. Once the gear design is complete, it will be printed using different polymer filaments for optimum comfort and fit. Then, the masks will undergo a filtration test to ensure proper mask seal. Finally, for the last two stages all the experimental data will be gathered and analyzed. Different production methods will be analyzed to determine the best way to manufacture the protective gear.
The masks created are meant to impact the Rio Grande Valley by improving current designs and to hinder the spread of the virus. As engineers we are looking forward to innovating, and if our findings can provide information to further advancements its part of our mission to bring this knowledge to who may need them. Finally, we will acquire the resources to start a research area in protective gear for epidemiological diseases. The outcome from this project will serve as a reference for possibly continuing work within the university's mechanical engineering department as a master’s degree project for further research.

PRESENT.TITLE: Development of Grapeseed oil-based nanolubricants using TiO2 nanoparticles as lubricant additives
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Recently, there has been growing concern regarding the use of petroleum-based lubricants. This concern has caused interest in readily biodegradable lubricants such as vegetable oils. The present study evaluates the lubrication performance of grapeseed oil modified with varying titanium dioxide (TiO<sub>2</sub>) nanoparticles of sizes 5, 18 and 40 nanometers as lubricant additives at different concentrations. The wear protection and friction characteristics of the oil-formulations were evaluated by means of block-on-ring sliding tests following the ASTM G-077-05 standard procedure. The experimental set up consisted in an AISI 52100 bearing steel alloy test ring rotating against an AISI 304 stainless steel block. During the sliding wear tests, nano-lubricants were placed in an oil bath chamber to allow constant lubrication, while the test ring rotated, covering it in lubricant by the action of centrifugal forces. The experimental results showed that the coefficient of friction decreased when adding 5, 18, and 40 nanometer particles by 83.95%, 62.82%, and 77.50% respectively. Furthermore, the volume loss was lowered by 77.80%, 82.19%, and 78.77% with the addition of the 5, 18, and 40 nanometer TiO<sub>2</sub> nanoparticles, respectively. Based on the experimental results it is concluded that modified grapeseed with the addition of different sized nanoparticles has the potential for use as a biodegradable lubricant. Additionally, this improvement in the lubrication could provide a longer life to machines with moving parts that require the use of lubricants, resulting in lower costs.

PRESENT.TITLE: Tribological Characterization of Vegetable Lubricants Reinforced with Halloysite Clay Nanotubes
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Manufacturing processes commonly use lubricants to decrease the friction between moving components, reducing vibration and improving the efficiency of the process. Usually these cutting fluids or lubricants are based on mineral oils and have additives which are not environmentally friendly, increasing the costs of the process from lubricant disposal. Therefore, there is an increasing need to employ environmentally friendly lubricants such as vegetable oils. Nanoparticles additives have also been studied in order to improve the tribological properties of these lubricants. In this study, lubricants of soy, corn, peanut and sunflower seed were additized with environmentally-friendly halloysite clay nanotubes in concentrations of0.01, 0.05, 0.10 wt.% by ultrasonication. Tribological properties were characterized under anti-wear and extreme-pressure conditions using a T-02 four-ball and a T-05 block-on-ring tribotesters. The results of this study demonstrate the potential of bio based nano-lubricants to be used in manufacturing processes.

The experimental results showed that the coefficient of friction decreased with the addition of SiO<sub>2</sub> and TiO<sub>2</sub> nanoparticles by 49.7% and 62.8%, respectively when compared to grapeseed oil without nanoparticle additives. In addition, the volume loss was lowered by 38.6% and 82.2%, with the addition of SiO<sub>2</sub> and TiO<sub>2</sub> nanoparticles, respectively. Based on the experimental results, it was concluded that modified grapeseed oil enhanced with nanoparticles has the potential for use as a good biodegradable lubricant. Additionally, this improvement in the lubrication could provide a longer life to machines with moving parts that require the use of lubricants, resulting in lower costs.

PRESENT.NAME: UTRGV COEC Engineering Week
PRESENT.TITLE: Design and development of a Pin-on-Disc tribometer for testing under extreme-pressures
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Tribotester is the general name given to a machine or device used to perform tests and simulations of wear, friction and lubrication which are the subject of the study of tribology. Tribological conditions in bulk metal forming processes are characterized by high contact pressures and large relative movements at high velocities between the tool and the workpiece. The present project is focused in the design and build of a pin-on-disc tribometer device capable to perform tribological tests under extreme-pressure conditions and to measure the wear and the coefficient of friction (COF) for a pair of materials, depending on the presence and kind of a lubricant, sliding velocity, and applied load. The pin-on-disc tribometer design consists in a drive system, a control system, a test chamber, a load arm, an extreme-load arm, a force sensor, and software for measurements and data acquisition. The tribosystem comprises a stationary pin (or ball) pressed at the required load against the disc rotating at the defined speed. The friction couple will be inserted in a test chamber. During the tests the following quantities will be measured: friction force, chamber temperature, rotational speed, and the number of disc revolutions (sliding distance). Technical specifications of the tribotester will be: nominal ball diameter of 9.525 mm, nominal disc diameter of 28.575 mm, sliding speed up to 500 rpm, and normal load up to 400 N. With the development of the proposed equipment, tribological tests could be conducted in accordance with the ASTM G99 standard.

PRESENT.NAME: UTRGV COEC Engineering Week
PRESENT.TITLE: Investigation into Tribological and Rheological Performance of Coconut Oil-based nano-lubricants
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Nowadays, global concern on the pollution created by conventional mineral have renewed interest in developing environment friendly lubricants derived from alternative sources such as vegetable oils. In the present study, tribological and rheological performance of coconut oil modified with nanoparticle additives was experimentally evaluated. The lubricant wear and friction characteristics were found using cross-cylinder and block on ring configurations. Two different nanoparticle additives were investigated: silicon dioxide (SiO<sub>2</sub>), and copper oxide (CuO). For the two conditions, nanoparticles were dispersed at different concentrations within the vegetable oil. Using a parallel plate rheometer, the rheological behavior for all the concentrations were analyzed. The experimental results showed that wear volume loss was lowered by 33% using both SiO<sub>2</sub> and CuO nanoparticles. Furthermore, the addition of SiO<sub>2</sub> and CuO nanoparticles decreased the coefficient of friction by 57% and 65% respectively as compared to coconut oil without nanoparticles. Based on this study it was concluded that coconut oil can be a potential alternative nano-lubricant for metal-forming processes that is biodegradable.

PRESENT.NAME: UTRGV COEC Engineering Week
PRESENT.TITLE: Micro-Texturing of UHMWPE to Increase the Longevity of Prosthetic Hip and Knee Replacements
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: After many years of repetitive stress and strain on human joints, bones start to break down and are in need of replacements. As a result, 1.25 million yearly joint surgeries are performed alone with the average patient age being 50-70 years old. Current methods allow for an average joint lifespan of ~7-15 years, which is influenced by complications such as excessive implant wear – one of the leading causes of joint dislocation and infection. As of today, joint replacements are made of smooth surfaced Ultra-High Molecular Weight Polyethylene (UHMWPE). It is believed that current methods help minimize wear rate, but novel studies suggest that micro-texturing the UHMWPE’s surface decreases wear rate even further increasing the longevity of the replacement. Surface textures allow for the collection of natural lubrication within themselves providing a cushioning effect against the adjacent joint. The texturing also serves as a pocket mechanism that collects joint-replacement debris keeping it from entering the bloodstream. Using a Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machine, a variety of polygonal geometries will be micro-machined onto the surface of the UHMWPE. Geometric parameters such polygon diameters, side lengths, shape spacing, and depth will be varied over multiple experimental runs to determine the optimal pattern configuration. Validation of the proposed pattern will be completed using a tribometer device with Ringer’s solution as lubricant. The gathered experimental data will then be analyzed in efforts to generate empirical models that will predict replacement longevity as a function of surface geometry.

PRESENT.NAME: 3rd Annual RGV STEM Education Conference
PRESENT.TITLE: Development of a new testing device to evaluate the durability of biocompatible materials and reach out RGV students within the STEM fields.
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: One of the main causes of hip prostheses failure is the premature wear of their components. Multi-directional motion or “cross-shear” motion has been identified as one of the most significant factors affecting the wear rate of UHMWPE in total hip joint replacement prostheses. To better evaluate the effect of this cross-shear motion on the tribological behavior of different biomaterials, a new wear testing device has been designed and developed. This new instrument is capable to reproduce the “cross-shear” effect with bidirectional motion on bearing materials and to determine coefficient of friction (COF) between surfaces during testing. To validate the functionality of this new testing platform, alumina balls were articulated against Ti-6Al-4V ELI alloy disks in Ringer’s solution. Four different articulation patterns, all with identical path lengths per cycle, were tested. Gravimetric weight loss was converted to volumetric wear data in order to determine the effects of motion patterns on the wear. Worn surfaces were analyzed by scanning electron microscopy. This scientific approach to quantifying the tribological effects of cross-shear provides fundamental data that are crucial in evaluating potential biomaterials for use in knee and hip joint replacements. In addition, the development of this new testing device will facilitate efforts at UTRGV to reach out students from traditionally under-represented groups within the science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) fields.

PRESENT.TITLE: Development of biodegradable nano-lubricants using coconut oil modified with nanoparticles as lubricant additives at UTRGV
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: In metal-forming processes, the use of lubricants for providing desirable tribological conditions at tool-workpiece interface is critical to increase the material formability and prolonging tool life. Nowadays, the depletion of crude oil reserves in the world and the global concern in protecting the environment from contamination have renewed interest in developing environment friendly lubricants derived from alternative sources such as vegetable oils. In the present study, the rheological and tribological behavior of coconut oil modified with nanoparticle additives was experimentally evaluated. Two different nanoparticle additives were investigated: silicon dioxide (SiO<sub>2</sub>), and copper oxide (CuO). For the two conditions, nanoparticles were dispersed at different concentrations within the coconut oil. The effects of concentration and shear rate on the viscosity were evaluated and the experimental data was compared with conventional models. A custom made tribotester was used to evaluate the effect of concentration on the tribological performance of the nano-lubricants. The experimental results showed that wear volume loss was lowered by 37% and 33% using SiO<sub>2</sub> and CuO nanoparticles respectively. Furthermore, the addition of SiO<sup>2</sup> and CuO nanoparticles decreased the coefficient of friction (COF) by 93.75% and 93.25% respectively as compared to coconut oil without nanoparticles. In addition, nano-lubrication projects at UTRGV will act as a vehicle to expose more UTRGV students to scientific research, to provide them with more opportunities to publish in scientific journals and present their work at symposiums, as well as to better prepare them to enter the STEM workforce and/or encourage them to pursue advanced degrees.
